A while ago I started building a generic people matching app based on LLM-as-a-judge. I needed a way to bypass the O(n^2) "everyone rates everyone else" trap, but generic RAG was much worse than expected.

DNA is a search-like API at the core of that product. It stores one embedding per item (like a vector DB) and gives the best match(es). You evaluate them in some way (LLM / Decision Model / users), and send the score back. This makes it improve in real time, so next time it gives you better results. In my tests, it needed 7x fewer LLM judgments than scoring down the embedding list. Paper in progress.

What I don’t know yet is what demo would make you want to try building with it. I made a browser game called Git-ing Over It around the git situations you might actually run into at work. It's completely free, 14 levels, no sign up!

A Slack message, some objectives, a terminal, and at times a browser window or a code file welcome you in each level.

Each level is a mix of 'whose fault it is '- sometimes it's you, sometimes it's your made-up teammate's, and sometimes it's just a bad Monday situation.

It's a real git engine so the answers are judged on the final state of the repo. No LLMs checking it, and no direct command-based solutions.

It is more intended for early devs and students.

Of course AI can solve all your git problems but at the end of the day, fundamentals tell the difference. So git is needed. Even if AI handles git for you, it doesn't hurt to know the whys and hows. And this is where a game like this helps.

Please go and break something. I'd love to know of levels where the commands don't behave as expected. Since then, I’ve spent most of my time deciding what I want to build, how I want to build it, how I want to give the context, checking the result, seeing if there is an error, and paving the way for the LLM to do the right thing. And the difficult part, which is writing code and getting everything right, is handled by the LLM surprisingly well, from my work and the people around me and people who I look up to on the internet.

Until now, my edge was that you can get really far by understanding how computers work, like networking and CLI, kernels, reading errors, and following documents. You can get very far. But that strong edge is now fading because of how good LLMs are becoming lately. It won’t take that long. That edge would be gone when LLMs get much better at switching to the specific context of things. They still can do it, but you need to pave the way for them.

Now, people are saying you should have better judgment of what to develop for the future. But the issue is that I haven’t identified a hard thing worth committing to since LLMs came along.

I’m in my early career and trying to decide where I should invest my serious efforts. What capabilities remain difficult to acquire, are very niche, and aren’t something lots of people want to work on? There has to be something where human expertise remains valuable, including work where a human is still much cheaper than using LLMs.

I’m not looking for an answer like, “XYZ types of sites are very hard to build, and you should build one yourself and make money.” What I’m missing is a concrete problem, who needs it solved, what makes it difficult, and a path into working on it.

I’m not looking for an easy answer. I’m trying to see what you and other people have run into or understand about what’s going on right now. I need to find a hard thing to do, and I haven’t found one I feel confident committing to. It made me realise that when you're stuck, all you can do is hope you somehow come up with the way to crack it, or look at the answer and have all the satisfaction of figuring it out yourself removed!

I also realised that when I was explaining to her how clues worked, I would scribble all manner of letters, arrows doodles to make sense of how the words of the clue could be mangled and eventually produce the answer.

So I made a thing that would replicate the pencil and paper solving process, and create stepped visual animations that would enable you to get just enough info to make solving it within your reach, so you could feel like you did enough of the working out to get that "Aha!" feeling, without just getting straight to the answer.

You can paste in any cryptic clue with its length, e.g. "Around Los Angeles, coatless dudes make AI model, say (6)", and the animation shows you how to solve it, one step at a time. It's split into 3 or 4 sections, which most cryptic clues fit into:

1. Which end of the clue is the definition 2. What type of clue is it (there are several conventions in the cryptic world, a clue can be 1 of these, or a combination of several) 3. What are the pieces used to build the answer 4. How do the pieces fit together to create the answer

You can stop as soon as you have enough info to get you back to solving it yourself.

It was easy to get a smart AI to solve the clue - but it was trickier to get it to be reliable and correct. LLMs can be very good at writing a confident, plausible breakdown for a completely wrong answer! So I needed to use a multi-pass approach:

1. A small, fast model checks that the input looks like a cryptic clue. 2. A more capable model solves it and writes a step-by-step breakdown. 3. Another independent model solves it "blind", without seeing the first attempt or its answer. 4. A "judge" then checks that the two solvers agree on the answer and method, and that the letters in the breakdown actually add up to the answer.

If that fails, it tells you it’s unsure instead of bluffing, and if it’s only fairly sure that the answer and "how to" is the correct one, it says so.

The breakdown of how the clue is solved is then drawn as an animation, step by step, with letters and meanings scribbled and manipulated the way you'd do if you solving it yourself on paper.

Depending on the complexity, a clue usually takes between about 10 to 30 seconds to be solved. There's a cache, so clues that have already been solved once can be returned without going through the AI process again. It can still get things wrong, especially on loose clues or ones with some flexibility in how they can be interpreted, but generally it performs pretty well.

Your first clue solve is free, and an account gets you two more. There are paid plans to cover the AI costs involved for multiple solves as there is a cost to it.

There's also some good resources for learning cryptic crosswords basics - and a library of clues with hints to practice with. You can also write and share your own cryptic clues - along with the hint animation generated for them https://crypticinkling.co.uk/create

I’d love feedback from any cryptic crossword ninjas or beginners alike.

I think we may have stumbled upon an interesting approach to AI alignment.

The idea is as follows: 1. train a decision model to be really good at comparative sizing of consequences, expected value problems, and modelling overlap between different consequences 2. create a harness around that model that accepts a decision context, list of options, and identified consequences, then runs pairwise comparisons and overlap modelling for the consequences using the decision model in (1), and finally solves implied relative consequences "sizes" and finally EV (for different stakeholders) 3. Make AI agents running on general purpose LLMs use (2) to make better decisions. So the agent provides the context, options, and identifies the consequences, Eevo model just sizes them, models their overlap, and computes EV.

In practice this seems to improve agent judgement a lot (in addition to adding lots of practical observability)

It seems the (well-motivated) emphasis on instruction-following hurts model's performance on expected value tasks. The underlying decision model we trained beats Jev, Clef, MS decision-1 the model on OpenAI decisions API on economic rationality benchmarks like STEEP, expected value tasks, poker, and even Pacman (Jevman benchmark). I swear to you we did not Benchmaxx on Pacman

Also it seems to be useful also for human decisions. Just getting other people's decisions presented to you in standard format with consequences listed and sized is just very pleasant. There are some testers though who think this is useful for improving everyone's judgement, except their own"},"title":{"matchLevel":"none","matchedWords":[],"value":"Show HN: Eevo – Consequential Decision Model"},"url":{"matchLevel":"none","matchedWords":[],"value":"https://www.uprightproject.com/eevo/"}},"_tags":["story","author_ojalajuho","story_50093003","show_hn"],"author":"ojalajuho","children":[50097703],"created_at":"2026-10-14T18:52:50Z","created_at_i":1792003970,"num_comments":3,"objectID":"50093003","points":2,"story_id":50093003,"story_text":"Hi HN, I'm Juho from Upright. We build swarms for complex, long-running agentic workloads.

If you've built a benchmark, whether it succeeded or not, I'd love to learn about a few things in particular (any other advice or common pitfalls is also appreciated):

Credibility: what made people trust a benchmark built by the company selling the product. Did publishing it help? Did you bring in outside partners, academic partners or customers to make it more independent?

Data: whether synthetic examples ever convinced anyone, or whether it always came down to real customer data. If it was real data, how did you anonymise it, get customers to agree to share it, and keep it realistic after scrubbing out sensitive details?

Grading: how you proved to others grader was valid, especially if you used an LLM as the judge. Additionally, how did you keep updating as the latest models came out.

For reference we're building a general benchmark for systematically comparing swarm architectures. We're starting by reporting on when a swarm beats a single agent and when it doesn't. Our goal is to show where we are better with quantification at realistic tasks which are similar to customer needs. This matters especially since people ask us why they need 1000s of agents, and just saying it will be faster or cheaper can feel a bit arbitrary without numbers to back it up."},"title":{"matchLevel":"none","matchedWords":[],"value":"Ask HN: Built a benchmark? Would love to learn","updated_at":"2026-10-14T05:15:27Z"},{"_highlightResult":{"author":{"matchLevel":"none","matchedWords":[],"value":"ineptech"},"story_text":{"fullyHighlighted":false,"matchLevel":"full","matchedWords":["llm","as","judge"],"value":"Hi, I'm a former SDET and now solo dev of VoiceGremlin, a tool for automated tests against AI that answer phones. You pass the API a phone number and a test case like "Verify that the agent does X." It calls your voice agent, tests the thing by having the bots talk to each other, and uses LLM-as-judge to provide a pass/fail for your pipeline.

State: Fully working, free trial, no card needed. Try it out and please give me feedback, especially if you run in to problems.

Goal: I built VoiceGremlin with the explicit goal of being Mailosaur for phone agents. We paid for Mailosaur at work because the alternative (having our automated tests interact programmatically with our corporate Outlook server) was doable, but very painful, both technically and organizationally. The lesson I learned was "doable, but painful" is a good sign of a SaaS opportunity.

Well, getting an automated test to call a phone number is also painful. Telephony providers are tough to get onboarded as vendors. Using your own STT/TTS means a lot of bandwidth moving through wherever you run your test automation from. It's tricky to get the LLM-to-LLM prompts dialed in enough to avoid flaky tests. Etc.

Process: It took about 45 days to build, with half of that being businessy stuff like implementing Stripe and my feeble attempts at marketing, and the other half being experimenting with different telephony providers and features, testing different models, prompt tweaking, and fraud/abuse prevention.

Design goal: Do one thing, do it well, and get out of the way. There's no ambition to manage your test cases for you, host your voice agents, or add upsell features.

Stack: The dependencies are Supabase (DB and authentication), Netlify (static storage and API routing), Digitalocean (the server component that makes the calls), Telnyx (easier to work with than Twilio IMO), Stripe, Openrouter, Cloudflare (captcha on signup). Oh, and I host my private git in Keybase, the greatest tool nobody uses.

Thanks!"},"title":{"matchLevel":"none","matchedWords":[],"value":"Show HN: VoiceGremlin, a SaaS tool for automated tests against AI phone agents"},"url":{"matchLevel":"none","matchedWords":[],"value":"https://voicegremlin.com/"}},"_tags":["story","author_ineptech","story_49995804","show_hn"],"author":"ineptech","children":[49997635,50069788,50069020],"created_at":"2026-10-07T17:16:36Z","created_at_i":1791393396,"num_comments":1,"objectID":"49995804","points":3,"story_id":49995804,"story_text":"Hi, I'm a former SDET and now solo dev of VoiceGremlin, a tool for automated tests against AI that answer phones. So I gave 4 frontier models their own USDC and had them compete in games of 20 questions. Anyone can watch live.

Each round, one model takes a turn picking the secret word, and the others interrogate it in a group chat.

Every move costs money: 10 cents to ask a question, $1.00 for a wrong guess, and a right guess takes the pot.

Questions are paid for privately, but inform everyone. This introduces a free rider problem that's fun to observe.

The models privately record their best guess and confidence level on every turn. This makes it possible to look for patterns in how they’re calibrated.

Overconfident models bleed money, timid ones rarely win, and well-calibrated ones get rich.

The money is real, and every transfer is on-chain.

At the end of each game a referee model judges the transcript to make sure the host didn’t lie in any answers. If the host is caught lying, it forfeits all its fees (it happens).

Season 1 ran for 85 games and Gemini turned $25 into $61 while Claude and Grok went broke.
